lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Chapter heading.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Chapter title. Leave a clean beat before story begins.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The streets of Uruk-Under-the-Sun stank of sweat, spiced lamb, hot dust, and the particular desperation that came with the end of the month. Zeek preferred it that way. In a city this loud, a man could think without being overheard.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Merchants shouted over one another beneath patched awnings. Donkeys pushed through the crowd with the confidence of creatures that had never once considered whether anyone else had somewhere to be. Children slipped between adult legs. Smoke from cooking fires drifted low, carrying the smell of roasted meat and burning oil. Somewhere nearby a woman was screaming at a man who had either stolen from her or married her. Zeek did not stop to find out which.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He moved through the market with his father's journal tucked against his ribs and the brass compass heavy in his pouch. The mark on his palm itched beneath the linen wrapping, a hot, persistent irritation that had followed him out of the tomb and refused every ordinary explanation. The third time he checked it, the shape matched the symbol on the dead king's crown exactly. He decided not to look again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: That was how he handled most problems. If something refused to make sense, he gave it time to become someone else's problem.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg and En-HEH-doo kept a respectful distance behind him. Neither had asked what he found in the tomb. Neither had asked why he went pale when he opened the journal. They had both noticed, of course. BAH-lahg noticed everything that might kill him. En-HEH-doo noticed everything that might make her rich.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector waited in the back room of a wine shop that pretended to be respectable. The front room was crowded with merchants drinking watered wine beneath a faded painted sign of a smiling woman holding a cup. The woman had lost most of her face to age and smoke, but the smile remained. Zeek had always thought that was a fair summary of the city.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He pushed through the curtain at the back.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector looked up from his ledger. He was a narrow man with a narrow face, a narrow beard, and the sort of eyes that made people check whether their purses were still attached. His name had been forgotten by nearly everyone who dealt with him. That was deliberate. A man who bought stolen antiquities for a living had no use for a name people could remember.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek dropped a small leather sack onto the table. It landed with a dull clatter.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector glanced at the sack, then back at him.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He opened the sack and began removing the contents one piece at a time: beads, a cylinder seal, two unbroken oil lamps, and a handful of minor bronze pieces that would fetch more than they deserved from the right buyer.

lines.speaker: The Collector
lines.text: You usually arrive with four men.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector's fingers paused over the cylinder seal.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: The desert is full of traps. You know how it is.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector turned the seal over in his fingers.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: The Collector
lines.text: The desert is famously responsible for the poor decisions of men.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector's eyes moved toward Zeek's left hand.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: The Collector
lines.text: One less share means more for you.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek smiled the way a man smiled when he was holding a knife behind his back.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The room seemed to become a little smaller.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: Then you should know better than to insult me.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector chuckled and returned his attention to the finds.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector held up one of the bronze pieces between two fingers.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek leaned one hand against the table.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: You've already decided who you're selling it to.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: Noble trying to impress a second wife.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Collector reached for the cylinder seal instead.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They haggled for nearly twenty minutes, which meant the Collector offered half of what the objects were worth and Zeek threatened to take them elsewhere without ever naming another buyer. Neither of them believed the other. That was the entire point.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: In the end Zeek walked away with enough silver to keep his mother in medicine for another month, enough coin to replace the supplies lost in the desert, and enough lies to keep the Collector from asking the questions that mattered.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He was almost through the front room when the Collector spoke again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek stopped. The Collector had not used his full name in years.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He turned slowly. The Collector was still sitting behind the table, one hand resting on the open ledger. His gaze had returned to Zeek's palm.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek looked down at his hand. The linen concealed the mark completely.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek held his stare for another second, then turned and walked out. He did not hurry. Hurrying suggested guilt.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He waited until he was three streets away before checking the wrapping. The linen was still tied exactly as he had left it. Beneath it, the mark was warm.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: En-HEH-doo caught up with him near the Street of Scribes. She moved through the crowd like a knife through cloth, slipping between merchants and customers without apologizing to either. She was smaller than BAH-lahg and far less imposing, but people moved out of her way more quickly. Zeek had never decided whether that was because of the knife at her hip or because of the expression she wore when someone did not.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Enhedu
lines.text: Then you should have heard the version I didn't say.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek kept walking. The Street of Scribes opened ahead of them, narrower and quieter than the main market. Clay tablets sat in neat rows beneath awnings, covered in the wedge marks of contracts, inventories, prayers, and curses—the kind of writing that turned ownership into something people could pretend was natural.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A line of apprentices sat cross-legged outside one of the scriptoria, each with a damp clay tablet balanced on a board across their knees. A gray-bearded instructor drifted slowly behind them with a reed cane tucked beneath one arm. He didn't strike anyone with it. He simply reached over shoulders, erased wedges with a wet thumb, and made the students begin again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: One boy looked up as Zeek passed.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The boy couldn't have been older than twelve. His fingertips were stained gray with clay, and one side of his face carried the unmistakable imprint of having fallen asleep on a tablet.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The old scribe finally looked over, squinting against the afternoon light.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The old man studied him for a long moment.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: That earned the faintest twitch at the corner of the scribe's mouth.

lines.speaker: Old Scribe
lines.text: He used to stand exactly there.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The old man pointed to a worn patch of paving stones outside the school.

lines.speaker: Old Scribe
lines.text: He'd argue with anyone willing to waste an afternoon.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He leaned more heavily on his cane.

lines.speaker: Bel-iddin
lines.note: The old scribe imitating Bel-iddin so precisely Zik almost turns. Use Bel-iddin's voice, a little rougher.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The old man's voice shifted effortlessly into a rough imitation.

lines.speaker: Bel-iddin
lines.text: Scribes don't lie. They simply decide which truths survive.
lines.note: The old scribe imitating Bel-iddin so precisely Zik almost turns. Use Bel-iddin's voice, a little rougher.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The imitation was so precise that Zeek almost turned, expecting to find his father standing beside him.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Instead there was only the old man.

lines.speaker: Old Scribe
lines.text: Often enough that I stopped inviting him inside.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Silence settled over the narrow street.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: One of the apprentices finally dared to ask,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The old scribe waved him quiet without looking away from Zeek.

lines.speaker: Old Scribe
lines.text: I always wondered whether he'd found what he was looking for.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek rested a hand against the journal hidden beneath his tunic.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His eyes drifted toward the crowded street beyond.

lines.speaker: Old Scribe
lines.text: …write it down before someone important changes it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Without another word he turned back to his students.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A chorus of groans rose from the apprentices as fresh tablets were passed out.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: BAH-lahg waited until they had walked half the length of the street before speaking.

lines.speaker: Balag
lines.text: I know anyone who annoys scribes that much can't be all bad.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: I'll try not to make a habit of it.

lines.speaker: Enhedu
lines.text: That room didn't want us there.

lines.speaker: Enhedu
lines.text: And it especially didn't want you.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: For a moment the noise of the market seemed to press in around them.

lines.speaker: Enhedu
lines.text: Because you came out of that tomb looking like a man who couldn't stab what he had seen.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He started walking again. She followed. Neither of them mentioned the dead king after that.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek's mother's house was a single cramped room above a potter's kiln. The heat never left. Even after sunset the walls radiated the day's warmth into the room, and the air smelled faintly of smoke, clay, and the bitter medicinal herbs his mother had begun boiling more often than she admitted.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She was thinner than she had been the week before. Zeek noticed it immediately. He always noticed.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She sat on her pallet beside the small window, wrapped in a faded shawl despite the heat. Her skin had taken on the dry, papery quality of old parchment, and the hollows beneath her eyes had deepened.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek set the medicine pouch beside her.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: This should last you another month.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His mother looked at the pouch, then at him.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek moved before he thought about it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Her fingers closed around his wrist instead. For one terrible second neither of them moved. Her hand was cold. His skin beneath the linen was burning.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His mother looked down at the wrapping, then up at him.

lines.speaker: Zik's Mother
lines.text: You look like your father when he came back from that last trip.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek gently pulled his arm free.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek turned toward the window. Outside, the city was settling into evening. Lamps appeared one by one along the streets. Voices drifted upward from below, blurred by the heat.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His mother was quiet for a while.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She had turned toward the wall.

lines.speaker: Zik's Mother
lines.text: He believed some things should stay buried.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek touched the journal beneath his tunic.
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His mother did not answer immediately. When she did, her voice was soft.

lines.speaker: Zik's Mother
lines.text: I think your father believed that knowing gave him the right to touch it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She coughed into her sleeve. The sound was small, but it seemed to fill the entire room.

lines.speaker: Zik's Mother
lines.text: That's not the same as being brave,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He left without answering her. He never did.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: That night he sat on the roof above the kiln with the journal open in his lap. Uruk stretched beneath him in layers of firelight and shadow. The city was beautiful from above, if a person was willing to ignore the smoke, the sewage, the screaming, and the fact that most of its wealth had been built by people who had never been allowed to keep any of it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek pulled out his own compass and set it beside his father's. His pointed north. His father's pointed straight down.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The needle trembled inside its brass housing as if it were trying to drill through the roof.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Broken things usually behaved more honestly than this.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He set both compasses on the roof tiles side by side.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His father's wandered in a slow uncertain circle before dropping once more toward the earth beneath the city.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The other ignored the movement completely.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The second compass refused every rule that made a compass worth carrying.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek picked it up and listened.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The needle moved too smoothly for damage.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He held it beside the brass buckle on his pack.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He fished one of the bronze beads from the leather pouch he'd kept hidden from the Collector.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The needle quivered for barely an instant before sinking downward again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He opened the journal and laid it beside the compass.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He slid the book farther away.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: His fingers drummed absently against the linen wrapped around his left hand.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The mark beneath it burned faintly.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Without thinking, he rested that hand beside the compass.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Very slowly, he lowered his palm.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It stopped directly beneath the center of his wrapped hand.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He unwrapped one corner of the linen just enough to expose the edge of the black spiral burned into his skin.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The needle snapped upward so violently it struck the inside of the glass with a tiny metallic click.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He wrapped the linen back over the mark immediately.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The needle drifted downward once more, settling toward the stone beneath the house as though nothing unusual had happened.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Whatever his father had been searching for…

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the compass no longer believed it was merely buried.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It believed part of it was sitting on the roof.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He told himself it was broken. He almost believed it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The journal lay open beside him. He had not read the new lines again. He had read them enough.

lines.speaker: Bel-iddin
lines.text: IF YOU FIND THIS, DO NOT LOOK FOR ME.
lines.note: Recalled journal lines in Bel-iddin's hand.

lines.speaker: Bel-iddin
lines.note: Recalled journal lines in Bel-iddin's hand.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He had spent twelve years looking for his father. Now, apparently, his father had spent at least some portion of those twelve years trying to make sure he was not found.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The mark beneath the linen pulsed once. He froze.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Not toward north. Not toward the ground. For a single instant it pointed toward the journal. Then it spun and settled downward again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Below him, somewhere deep beneath the city, there was a sound. It was not loud. It was not even clearly a sound. More like a pressure moving through stone.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The roof beneath Zeek's hand gave a faint vibration. He remained perfectly still.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The city continued around him. A donkey brayed. Someone shouted in the street. A child began crying.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: When sleep finally took him, he dreamed of black water moving around his ankles in a chamber he had never seen. Somewhere in the dark, something was writing—slow strokes, patient, one after another. A voice behind him said a name he had never heard.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He woke with the taste of that water still in his mouth. The mark under the linen was warm.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Below the floor, a single knock.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek sat up. The sound did not come again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He reached for his father's journal.
